utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, all. I'm Tom Hannis, along with Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no preliminary -- yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could the witness please be escorted back to the stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber and counsel would have indicated yesterday we are alive to your concerns, and we would, as the day progresses, accommodate you, as we sought to do yesterday. We were wondering whether you would prefer to have another chair than the one that you are now in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This chair is quite comfortable and I have asked for a higher chair in the witness room with a different kind of a seat, with a higher seat, and I think that the lady I was talking to actually understood what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So before I invite Mr. Hannis to resume his cross-examination, I give you the usual warning as to your solemn -- reminder as to your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'd like to start this morning by having a look at the video from the police parade on 30 March 1992, and I believe this is Exhibit 1D633. And I ask not to start at the beginning, but start at the point where the presenter introduces Mr. Cvijetic, who is going to administer the solemn declaration. And, first of all, can you tell me, if you know, who is that person who is doing the presenting at this moment? We'll start the video now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go forward then and play the portion where the solemn declaration is read out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The solemn declaration will be read by the minister of the interior of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija, Zoran Cvijetic. "I declare that I will perform the duty of authorised official conscientiously and responsibly, that I will abide by the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia and the law, and that I will protect the constitutionally-established order of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, rights, freedoms, and security, and that I will carry out these and other tasks and assignments of authorised official even in cases when carrying out these tasks and assignments would bring my life into jeopardy."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if we can put up on the screen for the witness now the transcript which has the solemn declaration. I understood that the video and the transcript were both marked with this exhibit number, so I'm not sure how it appears in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, at 1503, Mr. Macar, can you see the text of the solemn declaration that we just heard read out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think I recall from your OTP interview that you said you, yourself, did not take a solemn declaration for the new Serbian ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No one told you that you you needed to do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You are aware, aren't you, that some members of the former joint MUP of Bosnia, particularly non-Serbs, were released from work in various SJBs around Bosnia when they refused to take this new solemn declaration? You knew about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pre-war amendments to the Law on Internal Affairs envisaged that a solemn declaration had to be made. When I started work way back in 1977, the solemn declaration was made only by cadets who graduated from the police high school at Vrace. Even when the OTP investigators spoke with me, they asked me about that. They asked me whether I was aware of the fact that a solemn declaration had to be made, and I said that I was not aware of that. And I was a bit taken aback by the question. I couldn't tell whether it was provocative or not. And then I checked through some of my colleagues, in the meantime. They showed me some amendments to the Law on the Ministry of the Interior which envisaged that a solemn declaration had to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit P530. And I need to see Article 41, which is at the English 6. And I think it's the B/C/S page 6. It's tab 3 of our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is a Law on Internal Affairs that was promulgated in March of 1992. I think the Official Gazette date is the 23rd of March, 1992. You see Article 41 talks about authorised officials. And in the English, if we could go on a little further to the top of the right-hand column. It says: "The authorised official shall make a solemn declaration before the minister or an official ..." And if we can go further down in the English, you'll see the text. And can you see the text of the solemn declaration in your B/C/S version, Mr. Macar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it now. Yes, I can see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One difference from what is in the law and what was read out on the 30th of March, 1992, is in Sokolac. The language used was the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the established order of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; whereas, in the law itself, it just says the constitution and the republic. But other than that, would you agree with me that the text appears to be the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I have to object. The quoting of the transcript of the video is not entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If it's not entirely right, then it's up to the Defence. They put this document in. And if they put in the transcript that's incorrect, they should advise me before I'm relying on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. The transcript is perfectly all right, and it reflects what was said on that particular date. However, when you are reading the differences, you are not reading it all, that's the point. That's the point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we can all see both transcripts. Can you point out to me where I read something that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, it mentions Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Additionally, Yugoslavia is in what was read out in Sokolac, and that's not in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Macar, that those are the differences between what is in the law and what was said in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the partial difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to show you another solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit P510. This is the previous Law on Internal Affairs. This is tab 75 on the Prosecution's list. This was the Law on Internal Affairs from 29 January 1990, that was in effect up until this time. If we could look English page 12 and the B/C/S at page 5, Article 41, same article.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we've heard evidence during this trial with some people saying that they didn't understand what all the fuss was about the solemn declaration because it was identical to the old one. And, as far as I can understand, this 1990 version of the Law on Internal Affairs is the old solemn declaration. And I want to point out to you in the English upper right-hand column --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And also in Serbian upper right-hand column because it's showing the part which is not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll begin with the part that says: "That I will protect the constitutional order and the rights, freedoms, and security of working people and citizens with all my strength..." And I would indicate to you that this language of working people and citizens has been omitted from the new solemn declaration that's in the Law on Internal Affairs from March 23rd, 1992. Do you agree, or do you need me to take you back to the old law or the transcript from Sokolac? In neither place, I tell you, is that language about working people and citizens included, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that where it says here security of working people and citizens, this is communist terminology, communist language that was used, not only in this law but in many other laws. And here, you speak about citizens because I can't see why this difference should be made between the workers or working people and citizens because they are both citizens. So this is communist terminology that was just copied from one act to the other, from one legal instrument to the other, year in, year out. And it is very striking because people are divided into two categories, and then you have to ask yourself who are citizens, as opposed to the working people. If you look at this legal instrument and many other pre-war legal instruments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you can see that in subsequent laws, this kind of terminology was deleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing new is put in place in the new law. There's no reference to working people or to citizens or to anyone; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to check, but I think that the language is the security of citizens or something like that, but I'd have to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we put back up the transcript from the Sokolac video. It's 1D633.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see it there? My English says: "Rights, freedom, and security, and that I will carry out these and other tasks." There's no reference to anybody in terms of who those rights and freedoms apply to; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we were to launch a theoretical debate then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't want to launch a theoretical debate. Can you just answer my question. There's no reference to citizens or working persons or anybody; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But rights, freedoms and security cannot belong to objects --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Macar, I have to ask the question. You have to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Hannis, with all due respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request that counsel direct the Trial Chamber and not direct his remarks to he me, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness precisely answered Mr. Hannis' question. I don't understand why Mr. Hannis is protesting because the witness started answering his question, precisely what the question was, his answer was aimed at that. That is why I intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, apart from that, we can all read. It isn't there, but, I mean, we can all read. And, eventually, I would like the witness to take his headphones off and ask you what turns on it, because I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours -- Your Honours, I have a follow-up question to ask relating to the possible reasons that some people declined to take the new oath. And I'm going to suggest that one of the possibilities is because of the change in language. Now, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The absence of the citizens and the working class?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes and the addition of the Republic of Serbia ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The new republic ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, the addition and the omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That would have been hard-line communist, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, possibly, or someone who is just not comfortable with the change that he doesn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is the relevance to this case? I mean, the absence of the citizens and the working class?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, partly, Your Honour, it's because the Defence and certain Defence witnesses -- I think Mr. Zupljanin is quoted in a newspaper article that's in evidence somewhere as having saying there is absolutely no difference between the new solemn declaration and the old. That's not correct. There are differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Relevant differences? I mean, except for the fact that it's a new republic, and the republic now is called Republika Srpska. But is the omission relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it can be, because the new -- the change in the oath may have been the reasons that some people did not want to remain in a Serbian MUP. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the point I'm trying to make, Your Honour, is I ask a question whether it was in there or not. The response I got was something about having a theoretical discussion. And I disagree with my learned friend that the witness was answering my question. He was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you need the witness to answer the question to tell us what we can read?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but if he could take his headphones off for a second, I have a comment about that. Your Honour, the way a witness answers questions to one party, compared to the way he answers it to another party, is sometimes a factor the Trial Chamber can consider in deciding the credibility of that witness, the reliability of the witness, bias, motive, prejudice, and what weight to give his evidence. That's the point I'm trying to make there. Thank you. That's all I had to say before he puts his headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Macar, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look again at Exhibit P353. This is tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is one day after the Sokolac police parade. It's the 31st of March, 1992. And this is the dispatch sent by Mr. Mandic. Now, in the speech that Mr. Stanisic made in Sokolac, he claimed that the legality of the new Serbian MUP was based on the result of the negotiations of three ethnic communities under the auspices of the European community, and he says, provided by the constitution of the Serbian Republic and the Law on Internal Affairs recently adopted. Mr. Macar, you are aware, aren't you, that sometime between the 18th of March, 1992, and the 31st of March, 1992, Mr. Izetbegovic had withdrawn his signature to the so-called Sarajevo agreement, and as of at least 27 March, everyone knew that that agreement was not in effect? You knew about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when exactly Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew his signature. I do remember his famous statement, though, that he holds one opinion in the morning and another in the afternoon. I'm not sure when he withdrew his signature and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You are aware that on the 27th of March, there was a session of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in which Mr. Krajisnik informed the deputies that Mr. Izetbegovic, or at least the Muslims, were no longer going to follow the Sarajevo agreement, did you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What could be read or heard in the Sarajevo media is my only source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. In Sokolac, you mentioned that you spoke with Mr. Stanisic after his remarks. Who else was with him that day, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of people from Sokolac who were looking on. I had an opportunity to speak to Mr. Stanisic at the stadium. I don't exactly remember who was around him. I may be able to do so if I could look at the video once more. I was interested in this new MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the political implications of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I had thought about showing you the video and asking you if you could identify some people in there, but I think it will be better if I can do that later, because when we were trying to stop the video, the persons in the background were somewhat blurred. I'm going to see if we can get some better images to do that later on, perhaps tomorrow. Did you speak to anybody else who might have been travelling with Mr. Stanisic on that date, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said that after that you went back to work in Sarajevo. What time did you leave Sokolac and arrive in Sarajevo on that Monday?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took me about an hour of slow driving. And there were check-points of the Green Berets at the points of entry to Sarajevo, and there were also active duty and reserve police officers of the Stari Grad police station, so I took a roundabout route. I went directly to the city SUP, to Mr. Leutar's office. Because of the security-relevant events throughout March, we had this practice of meeting and discussing all the current problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And you mentioned, I think, that on the 31st of March, the day that Mr. Mandic sent out his dispatch, that there was a meeting in Mr. Leutar's office where he told you a little bit about what was happening in the MUP. Mr. Leutar is no longer alive; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately. He was a true professional. And, probably, even in the post-war period, he would have been able to make a great contribution to the work of the security authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know when and how he died?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was brutally killed in Sarajevo. An explosive device was planted under his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was after 1996, but I don't remember when it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You said that during these discussions, I think that Mr. Leutar told you that the headquarters of the Serbian ministry would be in the building of the former BH ministry. Does that mean the building where you were working in the beginning of 1992, the very same building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that the headquarters of the MUP of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the best of my knowledge, would be in the building of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that there would be something like a joint headquarters, that is, in the building of the Ministry of the Interior of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what building was it that you worked in, in January of 1992? What building was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the city Secretariat of the Interior on Augusta Cesarca Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned that Jozo had told you that there was going to be a new Croatian MUP, but that was going to be in Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that it would be established but that the preparations to establish a Croatian MUP had been completed, that those preparations had been made in Mostar for a MUP of the Croats, and that the equipping of that ministry with materiel and everything had been finished. He didn't say, however, where the headquarters of the ministry would be, because it was my understanding that the headquarters of all these ministries would be in the building of the MUP of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think it was on Berise Kovacevica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So all three ethnic MUPs in one building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you continued to go to work through the rest of that week, I think, until Friday, April 3rd; right? And you actually worked on April 3rd and then left about 4.00 that afternoon; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P29. It's tab 8 of the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is an article from the newspaper "Oslobodjenje" for the 1st of April, 1992. I see the photograph there, that's Mr. Stanisic apparently in Sokolac. And that looks like the event that we saw on video that you attended on the 30th of March; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph is too blurred for me to be able to tell. I can't really make out the faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you not recognise that that is Mico Stanisic in the photograph, in a raincoat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although he was much younger then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Weren't we all. You'll see the article below that, my English translation translates that as "April fool reality." And the bold entries, right below the big headline, says: "Serbian members of the service already invited to join 'Serbian MUP' Delimustafic sends his appeal for unity. The ones who leave - will be fired." You were there in Sarajevo, you must have known about all this going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me that there were so many security problems in the city of Sarajevo that I didn't have the opportunity to read this. You could read a lot of stuff in the papers those days, so I don't know whose comments these are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, just a few minutes ago, you told me you got all your information from the media; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I may have said that about something in particular, but I didn't receive all information from the media. Probably you asked me a specific question, and I answered that I was able to get some information from the media, most probably from television.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The invitation to join the Serbian MUP is a reference to Mr. Mandic's dispatch sent out on the 31st of March; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read the dispatch itself. It was addressed to the secretary. Mr. Leutar was present at the meeting who retold us the contents of the dispatch. Let me remind you that Mr. Stanisic informed me that structural talks about the co-ordination of the future ministry in that building that I mentioned were to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something that's in my English translation of the last paragraph of this article. It says: "The report of the commission for the abuse of the authority within MUP was announced yesterday. It says that the illegal burning of the confiscated money caused damage of 27.702.000 BiH dinars and that there were illegalities in the handling of temporary confiscated weapons and vehicles." Were you aware that there was some suspicion in circles that Momo Mandic had been involved in some of that? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P2320.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is at tab 79 of the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Leutar's immediate superior, your boss's boss?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the city Secretariat of the Interior of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And along the line of work in headquarters, who would have been his boss?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy and the minister, eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the deputy, by name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says here, it was Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever seen this document before? This is dated the 1st of April, 1992, and it appears to be from the full collegium of the ministry to the CSBs and the SUP Sarajevo and to all SJBs. Did you ever see it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was able to read it now. Bearing in mind the situation in the MUP and the functioning of the ministry, especially in 1991 and part of 1992, this dispatch seems ironic, or, well, let's put it another way, unprofessional.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Unprofessional in what way? It's from the collegium. It's signed by the minister. It's signed by the deputy minister. It's signed by all the heads of administration. The only one it's not signed by is Mico Stanisic who is listed as an advisor. In what way does this dispatch seem unprofessional?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tone down my assessment. Possibly somebody finally remembered that the ministry should start operating and doing its work because a year or so earlier, the functional system of that ministry was disrupted, and the ministry actually lost most of its remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In fact, this is a rapid response to the situation that has been created because of the memo sent by Mr. Mandic the day before, and I can show you if you need to, but I will tell you dispatch number 02-2482 of 31 March, 1992, as referred to in the document here, is Mr. Mandic's dispatch announcing the new Serbian MUP. So would you agree that Mr. Delimustafic and the collegium is trying to stop that process and calling upon all MUP employees to return to work and carry out their regular task no later than by tomorrow, the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the deepest intent was. I'm reading this at face value. But I would like to tell you, Your Honours, that sometime in mid-March, I had an opportunity to spend some time with Mr. Delimustafic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry, let me stop you there. That's not an answer to my question. That was not something that was informed in your 65 ter or the proofing note, as far as I know. It's not something that I want to go into at the moment. Perhaps Mr. Zecevic or the Judges may ask you about it. So you did not see this, but you see Mr. Mandic's signature is on this document as well; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as we noted, there is no signature from Mr. Stanisic on this first 1st of April document. Let me show you something that may provide an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at P171 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is this a convenient point before you go on to another document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm sorry, I missed the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we take the break and return in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put up Exhibit P171, please. And top middle, I want to focus on in the B/C/S. If we can enlarge the upper half of the page, those two middle columns. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this is from a publication called "Glas," dated the 1st of April, 1992. And the particular article is one that my English translation reads as "Inspection of Units in Trebinje." It's from the Tanjug agency, reporting that on this date Mico Stanisic, minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic, was in Trebinje where the SAO Herzegovina police and Special Police Units were established on that date. Did you know about Mr. Stanisic being in Trebinje on the 1st of April for what looks like a similar event to the one you saw in Sokolac on the 30th of March?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of him visiting any other SAOs for similar events in late March or early April 1992, or is the Sokolac one the only one you have any knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only am aware of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If, indeed, as this article indicates, he was in Trebinje on the 1st of April, that would be a reason why his signature was not on that 1 April dispatch from the collegium that we looked at just before the break; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first question is whether he was invited to the meeting. Well, I can't really speculate on the basis of this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to your testimony last week, at page 22.848 in the transcript. You were talking about the events of Friday, April 3rd. And you said that at about 1400 hours that day you went to Mr. Leutar's office, and that he took you aside and spoke with you, and told you that there had been a meeting of the leading Muslims in the MUP at headquarters and that they had decided at that meeting to arrest a total of 14 ethnic Serbs in leading positions in the MUP; is that correct? Is that how you remember it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say senior Muslim officers, but senior officers in the MUP headquarters who were of Muslim ethnicity, and the rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did he tell you the names of the 14 Serbs who were proposed to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave me the names. I remember some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I think last week you mentioned Tomo Kovac, Kukobat; is that correct? That's a name I'm not familiar with. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kukobat - you probably have it in your materials - was the chief of the crime service in the public Security Services Centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned last week, yourself and Mr. Planojevic. But I think in your e-mail from March of this year, you also mentioned Mico Stanisic and Mr. Kijac; is that right? Do you remember them being among the 14?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Momo Mandic? He seems like a likely candidate. Do you remember if his name was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him mentioning the name of Mr. Mandic, out of the 14 names that I remember. Well, it's been 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you all 14 names or only some?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember, because when I heard my own name, quite naturally this would come as a surprise for anyone, and then he -- I can't really tell you whether he mentioned all 14 names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, from what I read in your testimony earlier last week and in your e-mail about these events, it seems like this was a meeting that happened that very day, and Mr. Leutar has the information almost simultaneously, or within an hour of it actually happening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He didn't attend the meeting himself; right? He is a Croat. He wouldn't have been at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how he came by the information? Was there some eaves-dropping equipment in the office where the meeting was held? How did he know so quickly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jozo Leutar was very well informed as a senior officer, and he also had some friends among the Muslim personnel. Now, as to what channels he used to gain this information, I can't really speculate, but I do know that he was quite concerned and that the comment that he made after I sought some additional explanations from him, he said, well, he didn't know what to give me as a reason. He said something along the lines of, Look at those fools, what are they doing? And this is something that's really is etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You never saw any document about this meeting or the 14 of you who were supposed to be arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already explained, on that day, the 3rd of April, sometime around 1400 hours, I went to Sokolac with my late wife to visit my children and my parents. And after that, I could not go back to Sarajevo. I wasn't in Sarajevo anymore in order to be able to learn anything more about this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand your testimony from last week, you -- although they attempted to stop you at the check-point, you did not stop; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because my policeman's honour did not allow me to be checked by the Green Berets, paramilitaries. I actually was able to recognise a small-time criminal from Bascarsija in their ranks, together with the active and reserve police from the Stari Grad police station. They were all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you concerned that you might actually be arrested if you had stopped?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I was concerned, and it's not that I was concerned only about possible arrest. The way they held their automatic rifles, the people who manned the check-point, this could have resulted in some undesirable consequences. But at the same time, I assumed because there were many civilians there passing through, I thought that they would not use their weapons. My wife was panicked and quite upset, and she even told me to stop because she could not believe what was going on. She was able to see that they were removing clothes, pillows, bed covers from the trunks of the cars of those people, whatever it was that those people were carrying in their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you take it seriously at the time that there was a plan to arrest you and 13 other Serbs? Did you actually think that somebody was going to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information that I received at that level from this kind of senior officer is definitely something that should concern you, but I think that I was more focused on trying to find out what was behind all that. Unfortunately, it turn out that this information was, indeed, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you talk to any of the other Serbs who were supposedly on the list that Friday or that weekend, to see what they knew about it, Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Kijac, Mr. Planojevic? Talk to any of them to see what they knew about this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, Mr. Leutar, knowing that Secretary Kijac was not in his office, took me to his office in order to share this information with me because there were some other people in Leutar's office. Now, private telephone numbers that belonged to Mr. Kijac or Mr. Stanisic, I did not have those numbers in order to be able to communicate with them and my rule of thumb was always to socialise less with the police officers. And there were very few of those people whose home phone numbers I knew and whom I socialised with, because in the official communication, we had the duty centre where we could leave messages and try to contact people for official business. And I did plan for Sunday evening because I had some -- or, rather, my wife had some obligations in the Ministry of Finance where she worked, and I also had my own job, and I planned to go back to Sarajevo on Sunday evening. And our usual practice was that whenever we went to visit our children, to leave on Friday, unless there were some emergencies, and to go back on Sunday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall you testified about that last week. And that's a little puzzling to me. If you took it seriously that there was a plan to arrest you, why would you go back to work on Monday?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not feel any kind of guilt on any grounds, and I thought that I would be able to face all those problems. I knew that there was no legal basis for any kind of treatment of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear while you were in Sokolac about the attack or take-over of the Vrace police school by Mr. Mandic, Momo Mandic, and others from the Serb police force?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information about that from TV. I don't know what day it was. I think it may have been Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that one of the reasons you didn't go back to Sarajevo on Monday?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I received a report that traffic was disrupted on the roads leading into and out of Sarajevo on the Sokolac-Sarajevo route, and also after I received some additional information from Mr. Nujic, I did not go. My wife called her ministry, I think the minister at that time was Mr. Pajic, and he advised us not to travel to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If there had been an active warrant for your arrest or an all-points bulletin, don't you think that Sokolac would have been one of the first places the police would have looked for you, knowing that you were from there and your parents were from there? That kind of information must have been in your personnel file in the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are now talking about the time when the Ministry of the Interior functioned normally, then the answer to your question is yes; but if you are now talking about the ministry as it functioned in this time-period, where the ministry, in fact, operated in contravention of the Law on Internal Affairs and other legal frameworks, then the measures could have been ordered by a smaller circle within the Ministry of the Interior and taken also in that smaller circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And someone knew how to contact you by phone in Sokolac because Mr. Nujic called you that Monday morning; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in line with the procedure, all senior officers, including myself, had their numbers on their files. And, usually, I would say to the duty officer, I'm going to visit my parents, and my parents' number was there on the file, and they were able to contact me. And this is how Mr. Nujic, because, after all, I did not make it a secret that I was going to visit my parents and my children, that's how he knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned at page 22.856 from last week that starting from Monday and Tuesday, I guess that would be April 6th and 7th: "Many people came to Sokolac, a couple thousand. They had all fled. Among them were also my relatives." Where had these people come from that were fleeing to Sokolac? Had they come from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, from Gorazde. Especially my mother's family lived in the Gorazde area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so they had managed to get to --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And some of the family members were from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And they managed to get through the roadblocks, out of Sarajevo, on Monday and Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Sokolac-Sarajevo route, they could not. I know that a family past through Olovo, bypassing the main road, and managed to reach Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you, some time after this, went to -- well, where did you go first? Did you go to Vrace or Pale when you began to work with the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Pale, and then a day or two later, I went to Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned in Pale you went to a facility whose name I have a hard time pronouncing, Buducnost, Buducnost. Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that this is what it was called. It was a scout's hall, a small building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sometime I've heard reference to a Kalovita Brda, is that the same facility, or is that something else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked some questions about the inspectors who were working for you when you began with the RS MUP. You mentioned Mr. Kovac, Ljubomir; Mr. Orasanin; a Kapetanovic. Do you recall when Ostoja Minic was hired and began working as an inspector? I think you said in August 1992. But we've seen from the documents that he participated in the interviews of some of the Yellow Wasps who had been arrested at the very end of July, so do you know if he started before the Yellow Wasps had been arrested, or was it only at that very same time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite specific. Mr. Ostoja Minic was tasked with assisting in the prosecution of the Yellow Wasp cases in Bijeljina. And if my memory serves me right, Ostoja Minic used to work in the CSB in Tuzla, but then he fled to Bijeljina. I think for awhile he was in the military police and then he was transferred to the public security station in Bijeljina. And once a team was set up that would deal with the Yellow Wasps case, Mr. Minic was in that team. And that's how he actually became part of that group and he went on working in the crime enforcement division from August 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you said that there were four or five inspectors working for you in the time-period from April to the end of July. I want to ask about that, starting, first of all, by looking at one of the payroll documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 1D570.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that will be up on the screen in a moment, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's tab 18 of the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see this appears to be a payroll for the crime administration. Mr. Planojevic is listed as the assistant minister, and you are the co-ordinator. Inspectors include Mr. Milanovic, Mr. Orasanin. Petko Pekic's name is on here, but it says he was on sick leave. Do you recall that? Did he work any part of that time, or was he sick the whole time? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Further down, we see Danilo Vukovic listed as an inspector. And Sinisa Karan, I don't see a designation for him, was he working as an inspector at that time? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sinisa Karan was an inspector. I don't remember the exact date when he joined the MUP. What Mr. Vukovic and Mr. Andan, I think -- he was sent to Bijeljina to help out the SJB and to assist in the efforts to set up a Bijeljina CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And the bottom right, we see what appears to be the name and a signature, the name of Dragan Andan. What was his position at the time? Was he inspector working in your administration, or was he in some kind of independent position? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't work in my administration, and I wouldn't speculate now in which administration he did work. This signature means that he received the salary of Mr. Vukovic who was in Bijeljina. And I believe that these salaries were paid out retroactively when the budget was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. We see some dates by some of these salaries, seems they paid on the 28th of July for Mr. Karan. And then there's a note about travel orders for Mr. Planojevic, and you, Orasanin, Pekic, and Vukovic. What was that about? Is that extra pay you get when you travel out on your inspection tours or work-related duties?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the budget was set up, and I can see that it was in July or so, there were these symbolic fees. If you were to convert that into euros, it would be a negligible amount. So we did get some money when we were out in the field, but it was very little converted into German marks at the time, or euros nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I understand the higher the number, the more travel you were doing; right? So, for example, we see you got 10.000 which was more than your entire regular monthly amount of 8.500. Mr. Orasanin got 2.000, does that mean that you travelled five times as many places or as many miles as he did? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mean that. If there were other inspectors with me, I also received the money to cover some of their expenses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what travel you personally did in June 1992, where you went?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been 20 years, so, really, if you could remind me of a particular event, that would jog my memory, but otherwise. And, generally speaking, in the crime enforcement administration - I apologise if I interrupted you - there were orderly records of travel orders for vehicles and persons. We were very precise about it, as if it were peacetime. We did so because at some check-points, especially military check-points, there were problems with passing through. We had to show our IDs and prove who we were, and so on. Most of us at the time didn't wear uniform, especially crime enforcement inspectors. We also used our old official IDs until new ones were made. And if you had a travel order, you could show very accurately where you were and when. And let me add the following: We mostly travelled through war-affected areas or areas where there had been incidents involving weapons, so we needed some sort of evidence for where we were in case of possible consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's fair enough, Mr. Macar, I'm not sure where I travelled in June of 2011 much less June of 1992. I want to show you another document. This is tab 25 of the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 20149.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is another payroll document. It appears to be for July 1992. Yeah, the first name on the list as assistant minister is Mr. Planojevic, but then I see there's a line drawn through his name. We've heard evidence, and I understand, that sometime around the 22nd, 23rd of July, Mr. Planojevic was relieved of his position as assistant minister. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this mistake was corrected and that Mr. Planojevic received his due for the period when he was in his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, it seemed like he was entitled for payment for at least three-quarters of the month, but do you recall that he was replaced or removed from that position toward the end of July?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was replaced or transferred to another position in agreement with the minister is something I don't know. I think that there was some sort of agreement under which he voluntarily left the position of assistant minister and immediately was transferred to the State Security Service or national security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about it? Did Mr. Planojevic, himself, ever tell you about any disagreement he had with Mico Stanisic that led up to his leaving his position as assistant minister for the crime administration? What do you know about that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic and I had good relations. Initially, we planned together and made some pioneer arrangements for the setting up of the ministry. During this period -- but I don't know if this is fit for open session because it has do with Mr. Planojevic's private life. After ten years, he got a child. His wife was at Herceg Novi which is in Montenegro, and I believe that she gave birth there. At the same time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Should we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can. I know the witness has testified about it, but I don't remember if it was in open session when we heard about this before. Out of an abundance of caution, we can and then we can open it up later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we would do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, returning to the document, we see your name and the title is "co-ordinator," but co-ordinator has been scratched out. Is that to reflect the fact that when Mr. Planojevic has left his position you now are the assistant or acting assistant? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was still co-ordinator. This is late July or thereabouts. That is -- or, rather, why the word co-ordinator was struck out, I don't know. It may have been out of revolt or any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But who took over Mr. Planojevic's position when he left?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After August, that is, in early September, when the decision was made to move the ministry to Bijeljina, upon the request of the minister, I worked as a co-ordinator, and I was tasked to organise a crime enforcement administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you had been working as co-ordinator up to this point, was that a change, then, in your position or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, my appointment was still in force, appointment to the position of co-ordinator. But I got an oral order from the minister to set up the ministry, and I actually acted as chief, too, but there was no decision on my appointment to the position of chief. So you can check that in the documents. It never says that I was chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that you didn't get an official written appointment, but there was nobody else doing that job, de facto you were the one acting in that position; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it looks like everyone's salaries have gone up since the last month. Now instead of 8.500, you are getting 20.000, correct, at least on paper?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in 1991 and in 1992, there was high inflation. So in order to compare, you would have to convert the respective amounts to German marks, and then you would find that the salaries were approximately the same. You probably know that inflation was such that the exchange rate was set almost hourly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The number of inspectors -- we see some new names here that weren't seen on the previous list. I don't believe Tadija Cvoro was an inspector previously. Is that a new one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tadija Cvoro was an experienced police officer from before the war, and I believe that he was a reserve police officer because he had retired before that. We employed him for certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Radivoje Stanisic, Zeljko Vasiljevic, those were new ones as well from the last pay period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasiljevic was wounded in combat in the early days of the war, and he was treated in military hospital. His leg was badly injured, and he was on sick leave. And then we had consultations and decided that he should remain on the list until the final outcome that would take into consideration his medical -- or his state of health. And Ranka Vasiljevic, if you want me to explain, was a very good administrator, court administrator in Sarajevo. That's why we hired him in the administration as an administrator because we needed his profile, especially from September 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Stanisic's condition of being sick, I suppose that salary of only 6.000 is a reflection that he is not working full time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Radivoje Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radivoje Stanisic is an economist who worked in one of the audit services. We had no inspectors who had experience with white-collar crime, and by hiring Mr. Stanisic, we tried to make up for that. He may have been hired on the 15th or the 10th or the 20th, and that's -- that explains his salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document, and I note it's time for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we would resume in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, just before we start, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, may I respond on the question posed at the beginning, tomorrow, concerning the 54 bis? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I see you've got a new chair. Let us know if that causes you any problems. I want to show you one more payroll document before moving on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 20150 at our tab 44. I think the same document was on the Defence list as 65 ter 901D1 at their tab 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see there one, Mr. Macar, it appears -- it has a date 14 September at the top, but it appears to relate to salary for the month of August. Am I reading that correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I have a question: I know that at the beginning of August, you and several inspectors were doing a lot of work on the Yellow Wasp case, and Ostoja Minic, an inspector, worked on that case, and I don't see his name on that list, is that because he was an inspector working out of the CSB in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated, Ostoja Minic worked in the Bijeljina SJB because the Bijeljina CSB was not yet operational. The organisation was not yet in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have seen documents in April of 1992, and certainly prior to August 1992, purporting to come from the Bijeljina CSB, including input into the daily bulletin or daily report that was put out by the RS MUP. Did you not know about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm talking about the establishment of functions and organisational units in the Security Services Centre, I'm talking about it working at full capacity with all the sections from the crime police, the regular police, the financial affairs and personnel, and so on. That's what I'm talking about. And then you have to appoint people to the appropriate posts. Once you have done that, your centre is fully established in organisational terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, there's an intervention in the transcript. I don't think that it was properly recorded what the witness has just answered. The last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, your answer, the last sentence in English says: "Once you have done that, your centre is fully established in organisational terms." If you said something different, can you tell us what you meant it to say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not even an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then please repeat what you said, and we'll see if we get it correctly this time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief and as simple as possible. Once you appoint a person to the post of the centre chief, that does not mean that the centre is established in organisational terms. When I said that the centre was established much later, in late 1992, that means that the organisational units that are part of a Security Services Centre were established. All the auxiliary services, all the units, the crime enforcement section, the uniform police section, the analysis section, the financial affairs section, and at the time when I came to Bijeljina, this did not exist. And it was only when the ministry headquarters was set up there and when some personnel was re-assigned, it was possible to start building the CSB in Bijeljina, to set up some bare bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of Mr. Minic working on the Yellow Wasp case, how was that done in real life? He was not a member of your administration at headquarters. Did you draft him to do the work? Did you assign him? Did you request permission from the Bijeljina SJB chief? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was quite specific in my previous answers. I, and my colleagues from the crime enforcement section, did not assume the tasks of the SJB. We were in Bijeljina to assist the SJB in the Yellow Wasp case, and the SJB itself had its own crime service, and Mr. Ostoja Minic was part of that service. I don't know how long he had worked in that public security station because I have some information, according to which, he first served in the military and then transferred to the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. But was it the minister who sent you to Bijeljina to assist with the Yellow Wasp investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he made me responsible in that area which was within the purview of the crime police service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So Ostoja Minic, and whoever else from the local SJB was working on the investigation, would have been working under your direction for that task; is that right? Ostoja Minic wasn't going to be telling you what to do; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I caused a problem for myself by asking two questions, and when you gave me a short answer, it's not clear. So, was Ostoja Minic working under you for this task?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I co-ordinated work on the Yellow Wasp case. In that particular sphere, that was assigned to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before I forget the document that's on the screen, the September 14th payroll regarding August 1992, is that accurate, as far as you remember, as far as the inspectors that were working for you at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to correct you. They did not work for me, they worked in the Ministry of the Interior. Now, whether some of the names are missing or not, I can't really recall, but this would be, more or less, an accurate list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to quibble with you, but you are the number one on the list. If they weren't working for you, who were they working for? Weren't you the one that co-ordinated their work, assigned their task, sent them on inspection tours to wherever they got sent?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not privately in the MUP. Well, I'm not going to insist on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we can take a look at Exhibit P1252. This was shown to you by Mr. Zecevic last week. It's a document dated the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, it's not very legible. Could I get a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's tab 10 of the Defence binder. Let me see, I've got a hard copy that may be easier for you to read. I'll hand it to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were able to help us a little bit when talking about this document in terms of how documents were numbered within the RS MUP. And on this document, at the top above the date, above the heading, we have the number 10-18/92. Are you able to see that on your copy? It's above the typewritten date of 17 April.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you told us the number 10 referred to the administration for analysis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I assume, and I would be able to be even clearer if my memory could be jogged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it's my understanding that in these kind of numbers on the document, the first number does refer to the office or the administration from which it comes. And, for example, there will be a number for the administration for uniform police, and a different number for the administration for crime police, and a different number for communications and cryptographic protection; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you told us before that the number 01 would refer to the minister's office?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second number, the dash 18 before the slash 92, as I understand it, the 92 refers to the year in which this communication came from the analytical administration, and that number dash 18 would mean that was the 18th communication or document sent in 1992 by that administration; am I correct so far?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my administration, that is how things were done. If we sent a document at the request of the minister, and if we sign it for him, then the ordinal numbers followed each other, regardless of the fact that the minister had asked for this document to be drafted on his behalf. And now whether they divided their documents -- whether they made a distinction between documents sent by the section or by the administration and by the minister, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. Let me show you a different document and see if we can talk a little further about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D046, which is Prosecution tab 104, I believe, recently added to my list, Your Honours. I don't know if you received our e-mail for the last ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 15th of May, 1992, from Mico Stanisic. The number on this one is 01-1/92. And from what we've said before, it sounds like this is, sort of, the first one in 1992 from the minister himself or from the minister's office. Do you have any reason to disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please look at the signature because I would like to see who sent this document, whether it was sent from the minister's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if we can go to the next page. I am sorry, I don't have a hard copy with me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the signature and the stamp at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would just like to check whether there's any indication as to how this was sent and the level of encryption and the urgency. If we could go back to the beginning of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doesn't seem to have any of that information on it, does it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here "strictly confidential." You can see that above this line, "strictly confidential mail." Strictly confidential correspondence did not -- was not logged in the regular logs, and perhaps this is the first strictly confidential document sent by the minister. I hope that I have been of some assistance to you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that is helpful because we have seen documents earlier than the 15th of May that appear to be coming from the minister or the minster's office. But what you are telling me now, it says that depending on their classification, they may be logged in a different book and get a different order, a numerical order. That makes sense? My question is: Have you, Mr. Macar, seen this document before today? Did you see it in 1992? And do you need us to scroll down through the whole thing? It's about the formation of a war --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to look at it in order for it to jog my memory. So if you could just scroll it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly. If we could do the lower half of this first page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let us know when you've read through number 6, and then we can go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to the second page and to the top half first. And could I have the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You finished?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go all the way to the bottom on the B/C/S so the witness can see to whom it was sent. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you receive this document in 1992? I know on the 15th of May you would not have been acting head of your administration, you were under Mr. Planojevic at the time, but I wonder, did you see it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in item number 9, you see it says: "In order to command and control the overall forces of the ministry, a staff shall be established comprising:" It lists various people; the minister of the interior as commander, and then it includes assistant ministers for crime, police, communications, materiel and finance as members, which I take it to mean Mr. Planojevic at the time would have been a member as the assistant minister for crime. Do you know did this staff ever meet, ever function in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this body ever functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At least you, yourself, never went to any meeting of such a staff; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. And, as far as I can recall, this order was issued as a consequence of the knowledge -- well, we have already said that the active and reserve police and the crime police was engaged in combat to an excessive extent, and sometimes you would have a situation where, side by side in a trench, you would have soldiers who had committed crimes or misdemeanours before the war and had been dealt with by the police, or were dealt with by the police during the war because of those crimes, such crimes and misdemeanours. And at the beginning, the police was under the command of the Republika Srpska army because it did not have its own structures. It did not have its platoons, companies with the command structure. But they were all mixed up, and they were all under the command structure of the Republika Srpska army. I know that there were many complaints about police officers from the crime police who objected to the fact that they were in the trenches fighting side by side with people whom they had had to deal with. And those people were now armed, and there was a great deal of fear among the police officers. And in the end this, among other things, led to setting up of an organisation. Once you had a sufficient number of people from the ministry to keep them in a single formation from the platoon up, to have their own command structure, to have assigned to them an area of responsibility and not to be all mixed up with the other forces. And that, I think, was one of the key reasons why this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But, in fairness to the army, isn't it true that some of them might have had a similar complaint about reserve police officers who were in the trench side by side with them, because some of those reserve police officers were criminals who had been guilty of offences before the fighting started? So some of the army soldiers might have complained about policemen, the same way policemen were complaining about some of the soldiers next to them in the trench; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you compare those two indicators, I think that the number of persons who joined the reserve police and who had committed crimes or misdemeanours was at the level of statistical error, if you compare it with the number of criminals who had had to join the army under the Law on the Armed Forces because the police was in existence from 1945 until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But a lot of the reserve police who were in the fighting were only very recently put into the police, correct, in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, there were standing orders to the centres and the stations to remove this personnel from the ranks of the police of the ministry, and this was done. I believe that there may have been some isolated cases. A soldier may have noticed somebody wearing a uniform that they were not supposed to be wearing. But if you compare the numbers, although there were some complaints, we responded. But if you compare it with the number of persons who had committed crimes or serious misdemeanours, well, it was thousands of times bigger, this figure. And this was not because the police was capricious or anything, but the police forces -- the policemen responded because of the factual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't want to have a prolonged argument with you about that. Let me put this in context chronologically. This is May the 15th. You are aware that on the 12th of May there was an Assembly session of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was at that Assembly session that the VRS, the Army of the Republika Srpska was created and announced; correct? On the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in early May, as far as I remember, but when you mention the Assembly, my memory -- it's easy for me to remember if you mention the place where the Assembly session was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present at that Assembly. I have already said that. I attended most Assembly sessions during the war. The reasons are clear, it's communication lines. I know that the VRS was set up during that period, although from the organisational point of view, we did have an army because there was the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to something else. On the 6th of July, at page 22.879, you were shown a document that is 1D635. It was Defence tab number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is dated the 22nd of April, 1992, from the federal Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could get a hard copy again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Zecevic can help. There's the Defence binder. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could enlarge the English on e-court. You recall this is a document where the federal authorities had a state commission for genocide and had sent this document apparently to the authorities in Republika Srpska asking for information concerning crimes against humanity. Do you remember looking at that the last week?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just curious about the formulation of this. In the first paragraph, it mentions: "The state commission for the collection of data for the verification of war crimes, crimes of genocide, and other crimes against humanity and international law committed against Serbs and other ethnicities during the armed conflict in Croatia and other parts of the country." Now, do you know why Serbs were singled out and identified specifically by name, and everyone else was lumped under "other ethnicities"?
